Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 37, verse 6–10:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven with an adornment, the stars﴾, the singling out of the nearest heaven for mention may have two meanings:

One of them: because it is specific to the world (al-dunya).

The second: because it is specific to what is visible, and His saying "with an adornment, the stars" is because some of the stars were created for adornment, and some of them were created for other than adornment.

ʿUqba ibn Ziyad related from Qatada, who said: The stars were created for three purposes: as projectiles against the devils, as a light by which one is guided, and as an adornment for the nearest heaven.

﴿And as protection from every rebellious devil﴾. In this there are two meanings:

One of them: meaning, by the stars, a protection from every devil; this was said by al-Suddi.

The second: that God, glorified is He, protected the heaven from every rebellious devil; this was said by Qatada.

Regarding al-marid (rebellious) there are three meanings:

One of them: the one who refuses (al-mumtani'), said by Ibn Bahr.

The second: the defiant (al-ati), derived from tamarrud (rebelliousness), which is ʿutuww (insolence).

The third: that he is the one stripped of good, from their saying: a tree that is marda' (bare), when it has been stripped of its leaves.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿They cannot listen to the exalted assembly﴾. In this there are two sayings:

One of them: that they were prevented by them from listening or eavesdropping; this was said by Qatada.

The second: that they eavesdrop but do not hear; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Regarding al-mala' al-a'la (the exalted assembly) there are two sayings:

One of them: the nearest heaven; this was said by Qatada.

(p-39) The second: the angels; this was said by al-Suddi.

﴿And they are pelted from every side﴾. Mujahid said: they are struck from every place, from their sides; and it was said: from the sides of the heaven.

﴿Repelled (duhuran)﴾. In this there are two interpretations:

One of them: being thrown into the Fire; this was said by Qatada.

The second: being driven away with meteors, which is the meaning of Mujahid's saying.

Ibn ʿIsa said: al-duhur is pushing away with force.

﴿And for them is a perpetual punishment (adhab wasib)﴾. In this there are two meanings:

One of them: enduring.

The second: that it is the punishment whose pain reaches the hearts, derived from al-wasab (affliction).

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Except one who snatches a snatch﴾. In this there are two interpretations:

One of them: except one who steals the hearing; this was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr, derived from ikhtitaf, which is swift seizing; and from it the swallow (al-khuttaf) was named.

The second: from one who leaps a leap; this was said by ʿAli ibn ʿIsa.

﴿Then a piercing flame pursues him﴾. In this there are two meanings:

One of them: that it is a flame of fire.

The second: that it is a star.

Regarding al-thaqib (piercing) there are six meanings:

One of them: that it is the one that pierces; this was said by Zayd al-Ruqashi.

The second: that it is the shining one; this was said by al-Dahhak.

The third: that it is the sharp one; related by Ibn ʿIsa.

The fourth: that it is the high one; this was said by al-Farra'.

The fifth: that it is the burning one; this was said by al-Suddi.

The sixth: that it is the one kindling, from their saying: "ithqub zanadaka," i.e., kindle your fire; this was said by Zayd ibn Aslam and al-Akhfash, and he recited the poet's verse:

؎ While a man is a piercing flame, time strikes its brightness and it is extinguished

(p-40) And ﴿illa﴾ here means "but" (lakin) according to Sibawayh.

It was also said: the flame burns them so that they are driven away from eavesdropping, and they do not die from it.

The Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 37, verses 11–19:

 His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿So ask them: are they more difficult to create, or those We have created?﴾ Regarding it there are two views:

One: "Ask them," said Qatadah, derived from the istifta' (seeking a legal ruling) of the mufti.

The second: "Argue with them as to which of them is more difficult to create," said al-Hasan.

﴿Or those We have created?﴾ Regarding it there are three opinions:

One: from among the heavens, the earth and the mountains, said Mujahid.

The second: from among the angels, said Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The third: from among the past nations, for they were destroyed though they were stronger in creation than them, related by Ibn Isa.

﴿Indeed We created them from sticky clay.﴾ Regarding it there are four interpretations. One: sticking (lasiq), said Ibn Abbas, and from it is the saying of Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him:

"Learn, for Allah has increased you in stature and in the goodly qualities, all of which are sticking to you."

The second: viscous (lazij), said Ikrimah.

The third: adhering (laziq), said Qatadah.

The difference between lasiq and laziq is that lasiq is that which has stuck part to part, while laziq is that which clings to whatever touches it.

The fourth: lazim (enduring/inseparable). The Arabs say "clay lazib" and "lazim," and al-Nabighah said:

"Do not think that good will come without any evil after it, nor think that evil is a stroke that will not stick."

This verse was revealed concerning Rukanah ibn Zayd ibn Hashim ibn Abd Manaf and Abu al-Ashudd ibn Usayd ibn Kilab al-Jumahi.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Rather, you wonder, and they mock.﴾ Regarding "you wonder" there are two recitations (qira'at):

The first: with a ḍamma on the tā' (ʿajibtu, "I wonder" in the passive/active sense of the speaker's wonder attributed to Allah), recited by Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, and it is the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud. Regarding the interpretation of this reading there are two views:

One: it means "rather, you have denied," related by al-Naqqash.

The second: it is the saying of Ali ibn Isa, that they have come to the position of one at whom wonder is directed.

The second recitation: with a fatḥa on the tā', recited by the rest of the readers, and it attributes the wondering to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, as if He said: "Rather, you wonder, O Muhammad," said Qatadah.

Regarding what he wondered at there are two views:

One: from the Qur'an when it was given to him, said Qatadah.

The second: from the truth that came to them, which they did not accept, and this is the meaning of the saying of Ibn Ziyad.

Regarding His saying ﴿and they mock﴾ there are two views:

One: at the Messenger when he invites them.

The second: at the Qur'an when it is recited to them.

One: when they are reminded with what was revealed of the Qur'an, they do not benefit, and this is the meaning of the saying of Qatadah.

The second: when they are reminded of those of the nations who perished, they do not take heed, and this is the meaning of what Sa'id related.

The second: what they witnessed of the destruction of the deniers, and this is a possibility.

It has been said that this was concerning Rukanah ibn Zayd and Abu al-Ashudd ibn Kilab.

God, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And they will say, "Woe to us! This is the Day of Judgment."﴾ (to the end of the verse).

On this there are two views:

First: it is the Day of Reckoning. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: it is the Day of Recompense. This is related from Qatadah.

﴿This is the Day of Decision﴾ (to the end of the verse).

On this there are two views:

First: it is the Day of judgment among the creation. This is related from Yahya.

Second: on it the truth is separated from falsehood. This is related from Ibn ʿIsa.

(p-43) God, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Gather those who did wrong﴾ (to the end of the verse).

On this there are three views:

First: those who denied the messengers.

Second: they are the shurta (the guards or police). This is related by al-Thawri.

Third: they are everyone who transgressed against the Creator and the created.

On ﴿and their spouses﴾ there are four views:

First: their likenesses, so the adulterer is gathered with the adulterer, and the drinker of wine with the drinker of wine. This is said by ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him.

Second: their companions. This is said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Third: their partisans (ashyaʿ). This is said by Qatadah, and from it is the verse of the poet:

"So the bull crouched in a meadow of wadi-grass and a verdant plot, its plants beautiful, covering its mates (al-azwaj)."

Fourth: their women who agreed with them in disbelief. This is narrated by al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him.

﴿Whom they used to worship﴾ ﴿besides Allah﴾. On who they are there are three opinions:

The Almighty's words: ﴿They will turn to one another, questioning each other﴾. There are two views concerning this:

One: the humans turn to the jinn. This is the view of Qatadah.

Two: some of them turn to others. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

It may also bear a third meaning: the followers turn to those they followed.

Regarding ﴿yatasa'alun﴾ (questioning one another), there are two interpretations:

One: they blame one another (yatalawamun). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

Two: they seek comfort from one another (yatawanasun). This interpretation is flawed, because seeking comfort is a form of relief, and there is no relief for the people of the Fire.

It may also bear a third meaning: the follower asks his leader to bear his punishment on his behalf.

The Almighty's words: ﴿You used to come to us from the right﴾. There are two views on the interpretation of this:

One: the humans said it to the jinn. This is the view of Qatadah.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 37, verse 38–49:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will be served with a cup from a flowing spring﴾, meaning, a cup of wine that flows (ma'in). Concerning this there are three opinions:

First: it is the flowing one. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Second: the one that does not cease, related by Juwaybir.

Third: it is the one that has not been pressed, said by Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah.

It may also bear a fourth meaning: that it is wine in its pure state, not mixed with anything else.

Concerning ma'in (flowing) as applied to water, there are five opinions:

First: that it is what is visible to the eye, said by al-Kalbi.

Second: that it is what springs flow with, continuous and never cut off, said by al-Hasan.

Third: that it is the one that runs strongly, from their saying "amʿana fi kadha" when one's entry into something becomes intense.

Fourth: that it is abundant, derived from ma'in, which means a great quantity.

(p-47) Fifth: that it is the one benefited from, derived from al-ma'un (that which is useful), said by al-Farra'.

﴿White, delicious to the drinkers﴾. This means that the wine of Paradise is white in colour, and in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is "yellow" (safra').

It may also be that the cup is white while the drink is yellow in colour, so that their difference in appearance is apparent. The poet said:

Their brightness and the brightness of their cup are like fire and light confined within a vessel.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿No headache therein﴾. Concerning this there are five interpretations:

First: that there is no headache in it, related by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: there is no stomach-ache in it, said by Mujahid.

Third: there is no harm in it, said by al-Farra' and 'Ikrimah. These three are close in meaning, since al-ghawl is derived from al-gha'ilah (harm).

Fourth: there is no sin in it, said by al-Kalbi.

Fifth: that it does not steal away their minds, said by al-Suddi and Abu 'Ubaydah, and from it is the poet's saying:

This is from the ghilah (ambush), that one should strike down another one by one.

﴿Nor will they be intoxicated by it﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations:

Of the maidens restraining their glances, if a tiny ant crept upon her cheek, it would leave a mark.

Concerning al-'in (wide-eyed) there are two opinions:

One: those with beautiful eyes, said by Mujahid and Muqatil.

Second: those with large eyes, said by al-Akhfash and Qutrub.

﴿As if they were hidden eggs﴾.

Concerning this there are two opinions:

One: it means pearls in their shell, said by Ibn 'Abbas, and from it is the poet's saying:

She is white like a pearl of the oyster, separated from a hidden jewel.

Second: it means eggs known in their shell, and al-maknun is the protected.

Concerning the comparison of them to hidden eggs, there are four opinions:

First: a comparison to ostrich eggs, which are sheltered by feathers from dust and wind, so they are white tending toward yellow, said by al-Hasan.

Second: a comparison to the inside of an egg when no hand has touched it, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Third: a comparison to the whiteness of an egg when its shell is removed, said by al-Suddi.

Fourth: a comparison to the membrane that lies between the outer shell and the inner part of the egg, said by 'Ata'.

**Al-Mawardi's commentary (al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun) on Surah 37, verses 50–61:**

The first: it is Satan, who used to lead him astray, but he did not obey him. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: it was a partner of his who used to call him to disbelief, but he did not respond. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: they are the two men in Surah al-Kahf, ﴿And strike for them an example of two men﴾, up to the end of their story, and the believer of the two said to the disbeliever, who was in the Fire, while he himself was in Paradise.

﴿He would say: "Are you indeed among those who affirm?"﴾: he means affirming the Resurrection.

One of them: "shall we indeed be called to account." This was said by Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi.

The second: "shall we indeed be requited," said by Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b, from his saying: "As you do, so shall you be done by."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 37, verses 75–82:

One of them: that Allah may purify the earth of the disobedient.

The second: that they may be an example, from which those after them among the nations may take admonition.

His saying: ﴿So excellent were the Responders﴾ may have two meanings. One of them: "So excellent were the Responders" to Nuh in his supplication.

The second: "So excellent were the Responders" to whoever calls upon them, because praising the generality of the response is more eloquent.

﴿And We saved him and his family﴾. Qatadah said: they were eight: Nuh, his three sons, and their wives—four men and four women.

﴿From the great distress﴾. In this there are two meanings:

One of them: from the drowning of the Flood. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: from the harm that used to befall him from his people. This was related by Ibn Isa.

﴿And We made his descendants the survivors﴾. Ibn Abbas said: all people after Nuh are from his descendants. His sons were three: Sam, Ham and Yafith. So the Arabs and the non-Arabs (ajam) are the children of Sam; the Romans, the Turks and the Slavs are the children of Yafith; and the Sudanese are among the children of Ham. The poet said:

"An old woman from the sons of Ham ibn Nuh, as if her forehead were the stone of the Maqam."

His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And We left for him among the later generations﴾. In this there are three meanings:

The first: its meaning is that Allah preserved a good remembrance for him among the later generations. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: a tongue of truthfulness for all the prophets. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: it is His saying ﴿Peace be upon Nuh among the worlds﴾. This was said by al-Farra'.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 37, verses 83–87:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying: ﴿And indeed, among his shī'a (party/followers) was Ibrahim﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

First: among the people of his religion. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: upon his method and his sunnah (way). This was said by Mujahid.

Regarding the root meaning of *shī'a* (party, followers) in the language, there are two views:

First: that they are the followers (*al-atbā'*). From this is the saying of the poet:

*"The companion said: tomorrow you will turn us away, or [your] shī'ah. Will you not escort us?"*

His saying *"or shī'ah"* means: the day that follows tomorrow. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

Second: this is the view of al-Asma'i, that *al-shī'ah* are the helpers. It is derived from *al-shiyā'*, which is the small pieces of firewood placed with the large ones until the fire is kindled, because it helps with the fuel (*al-waqūd*).

Then regarding it there are two views:

First: that among the *shī'ah* of Muhammad (ﷺ) was Ibrahim, peace be upon them both. This was said by al-Kalbi and al-Farra'.

Second: that among the *shī'ah* of Nuh was Ibrahim. This was said by Mujahid and Muqatil.

Regarding the name Ibrahim there are two views:

First: that it is a non-Arabic (*a'jamī*) name. This is the view of the majority.

Second: that it is derived from *al-barhamah*, which is the sustained gazing (*idāmat al-nazar*).

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying: ﴿When he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations:

First: free from doubt. This was said by Qatadah.

Second: free from shirk. This was said by al-Hasan.

Third: sincere (*mukhlis*). This was said by al-Dahhak.

(p-55) Fourth: that he was not one who curses much (*laʿʿān*). This was said by 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr.

The phrase *"his coming to his Lord"* may bear two meanings:

First: at the time of his calling [people] to His tawhid and obedience.

Second: at the time of his being cast into the fire.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 37, verses 88–98:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿So he glanced at the stars﴾. On this there are four interpretations:

The first: He saw a star rising, and by this he knew that it has a Creator God. This was his glancing at the stars. This was related by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.

The second: It is a phrase from the speech of the Arabs: when a man reflects upon his affair, they say, "He has glanced at the stars." This was related by Qatadah.

The third: He considered what was "najama" (came forth, emerged) from their saying. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The fourth: The knowledge of the stars was part of prophethood. When God, exalted is He, held back the sun for Yusha' ibn Nun (Joshua son of Nun), this knowledge was nullified. Thus Ibrahim's glancing at them was prophetic knowledge. This was related by Ibn A'ishah.

Juwaybir related from al-Dahhak that the knowledge of the stars remained until the time of 'Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon him, until they entered upon him in a place that was not discovered. Maryam said to them, "From where did you know its location?" They said, "From the stars." So at that point he supplicated to his Lord and said, "O God, confuse them in its knowledge, so that no one knows the knowledge of the stars." Thus its ruling became forbidden in the Sharia and its knowledge became unknown among the people.

Al-Kalbi said: They were in a village between Basra and Kufa called Hurmuzjird, and they used to look at the stars.

﴿So he said, "Indeed, I am sick."﴾ On this there are seven interpretations:

The first: He deduced from them the time of a fever that used to afflict him.

The second: "Sick" with the death that is in my neck.

The third: "Sick" with what I see of the ugliness of your deeds in worshipping other than God.

The fourth: "Sick" with his doubt.

The fifth: Due to his knowledge that He has a Creator God who is worthy of worship. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

The sixth: Due to an illness that befell him.

The seventh: Their king sent to him that tomorrow is our festival, so come out. He looked at a star and said, "Indeed, this star has never risen except that it rose with my sickness." So they turned away from him, retreating. This was said by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: The Prophet of God struggled concerning his religion, so he said, "Indeed, I am sick."

Sufyan said: They used to flee from the plague, so he wanted to be alone with their gods, and so he said, "Indeed, I am sick," meaning "plague-stricken." This is his sin about which he said, "Forgive me my sin on the Day of Recompense."

Abu Hurayrah related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Ibrahim did not lie except three times: two of them concerning the sake of God, the Mighty and Majestic: his saying, 'Indeed, I am sick,' and his saying, 'Rather, this, their chief, did it,' and his saying concerning Sarah, 'She is my sister.'"

﴿Then he turned to their gods﴾. On this there are four aspects:

The first: He went to them. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: He inclined toward them. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: He attacked them. This was said by al-Akhfash.

The fourth: He faced them. This was said by al-Kalbi and Qutrub, and this is close to the two meanings mentioned earlier.

﴿So he said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ On this there are two views. One: he said that mockingly to them. This was said by Ibn Ziyad.

The second: He found them, when they had gone out to their festival, having prepared food for their gods so that it would be blessed for them. Therefore he said to the idols, though they cannot understand his speech, as an argument against the ignorance of those who worship them,

and as an alert to their helplessness. For this reason he said: ﴿What is wrong with you that you do not speak?﴾ ﴿Then he turned upon them, striking with the right hand﴾. On this there are three interpretations:

The first: His right hand. This was said by al-Dahhak, because it is stronger and striking with it is more forceful.

The second: With the right hand (oath) with which he swore when he said, ﴿And by God, I will surely plot against your idols﴾. This was related by Ibn 'Isa.

The third: It means with strength, and the strength of prophethood is greater. This was said by Tha'lab.

﴿So they came toward him hastening﴾. On this there are five interpretations: The first: They went out. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: They ran. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The third: They slipped away stealthily. This was related by Ibn 'Isa.

The fourth: They trembled in anger. This was related by Yahya ibn Salam.

The fifth: They strutted, which is the walk of arrogance. Mujahid said this, and from it is derived "zifaf" (the escorting of the bride to her husband). Al-Farazdaq said:

"The lead camel came before its young ones, hastening, and behind it came the ones that were hastening."

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And God created you and what you make﴾. On this there are two aspects: One: that God created you and created your deeds. The second: He created you and created the idols that you fashioned.

﴿So they intended a scheme against him﴾, meaning burning him with the fire they had kindled for him.

﴿So We made them the lowest﴾. On this there are four aspects: The first: the lowest in the fire of Hell. This was said by Yahya. The second: the lowest in the refutation of the argument. Qatadah said: So they did not debate with him after that until they were destroyed. The third: meaning the ones who were destroyed, for God, exalted is He, followed that with their destruction. The fourth: the ones subdued for the deliverance of Ibrahim from their scheme.

Ka'b said: On that day no one among the people benefited from the fire, and what it burned of him that day was only his bonds.

Umm Subabah al-Ansariyyah related from 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, that the Messenger of God ﷺ told her: "When Ibrahim was thrown into the fire, all the creatures were extinguishing the fire from him except the gecko, for it was blowing upon it." So the Messenger of God ﷺ commanded that it be killed.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 37, verses 99–113:**

The first view: he said, when he was thrown into the fire, and on this view there are two interpretations:

The first: "I am going to where my Lord has decreed for me."

The second: "I am dying," as one says of someone who has died, "he has gone to Allah, exalted is He." For he, peace be upon him, imagined that he would die by being cast into the fire, according to what was customary for it in destroying whatever was thrown into it, until it was said to it: ﴿O fire, be cool and safe﴾. Then Abraham was saved from it.

Regarding His words, ﴿He will guide me﴾, on this view there are two interpretations:

The first: He will guide me to deliverance from the fire.

The second: to Paradise.

What Abraham said could carry two meanings:

The first: that by his words addressed to the one who threw him into the fire, this would be a warning to them.

The second: that by his words addressed to those among the people who were present and witnessed him, this would be from him a warning to them. This is the interpretation of that according to the view of those who mention that he said it before being thrown into the fire.

The second view: that he said it after his emergence from the fire.

﴿I am going to my Lord﴾. On this view there are three interpretations:

The first: "I am devoted to Allah through my worship," related by al-Naqqash.

The second: "I am going to Him with my heart, my religion and my deeds," said by Qatadah.

The third: "I am emigrating to Him with my self," so he emigrated from the land of Iraq.

Muqatil said: he was the first of creation to emigrate, together with Lot and Sarah.

As for the land to which he emigrated, there are two views: the first, to the land of al-Sham (Syria).

The second, to the land of Harran, related by al-Nasa'i.

Regarding His words, ﴿He will guide me﴾, on this view there are two interpretations:

The first: He will guide me to the words: "Allah is sufficient for me; in Him I put my trust," said by Sulayman.

The second: to the path of emigration, said by Yahya.

This statement of his could carry two meanings:

The first: that by his words addressed to the one who separated from him among his people, this would be a rebuke to them.

The second: that by his words addressed to the one who emigrated with him from his family, this would be from him an encouragement.

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿So We gave him good news of a forbearing boy﴾, meaning: dignified and grave.

Al-Hasan said: "I have never heard that Allah makes lawful for His servants anything more glorious than forbearance."

On this there are two views:

The first: that he is Isaac. Allah, exalted is He, praised no one for forbearance except Isaac and Abraham, said by Qatadah.

The second: that he is Ishmael, and the good news of Isaac's prophethood came after that, said by Amir al-Sha'bi.

Al-Kalbi said: Ishmael was thirteen years older than Isaac.

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And when he reached the age of striving with him﴾. On this there are four aspects:

The first: that he walked with his father, said by Qatadah.

The second: that he reached the age of work with him, said by Ikrimah.

The third: that it is the striving of work by which proof is established, said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: that it is the striving in worship, said by Ibn Zayd.

Ibn 'Abbas said: he fasted and prayed. Have you not heard Allah saying: ﴿and strives for it its striving﴾ [al-Isra' 19]. Al-Farra' and al-Kalbi said: he was thirteen years old on that day.

﴿He said, "O my son, I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you"﴾. Simak related from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The dreams of the prophets are revelation."

﴿So see what you think﴾. He did not say this to him in the manner of consultation regarding the command of Allah, glorified is He. On this there are three aspects:

The first: that he said it to inform him of what Allah, exalted is He, had commanded him, so that he would be more obedient to Him.

The second: that he said it as a test of his patience in the command of Allah, exalted is He.

The third: meaning, "what do you show me of your patience or your distress?" said by al-Farra'.

﴿He said, "O my father, do what you are commanded"﴾, the verse.

On this there are two aspects:

The first: concerning the slaughter, said by Muqatil.

The second: concerning the decree, related by al-Kalbi. So he found him in the test sincere in obedience, swift in response, strong in religion.

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿So when they had both submitted﴾. On this there are two aspects:

The first: that they agreed upon one matter, said by Abu Salih.

The second: that they both surrendered the matter to Allah, exalted is He, which is the view of al-Suddi.

Qatadah said: Ishmael surrendered himself to Allah, and Abraham surrendered his son to Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And he put him down upon his forehead﴾. On this there are three aspects:

The first: its meaning is that he threw him down upon his brow (jabin), said by Ibn 'Abbas. The jabin is the area on either side of the forehead (jabha). The poet said:

"And Abu Hakam put him down upon the brow, so he went to his mother, the abyss."

The second: that he laid him down on his face, said by Mujahid.

The third: that he placed his forehead upon a hillock, said by Qutrub.

Mujahid related from Isaac that he said: "O my father, slaughter me while I am prostrate, and do not look at my face, for perhaps you will have mercy on me and not slaughter me."

﴿And We called to him, "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision"﴾: that is, you did what you saw in the dream. Regarding what he saw, there are three views:

The first: that what he saw was that he took the position of the slaughterer, waiting for the command to carry out the slaughter.

The second: that what he saw was that he was commanded to slaughter him on condition of being empowered, but he was not empowered over him, for it is reported that whenever he struck with the blade, it turned back, and he placed a sheet of copper upon his throat.

The third: that what he saw was that he slaughtered him, and he had indeed done so, but Allah, exalted is He, joined the veins without a separation.

﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾ by pardoning the slaughter of his son.

Regarding the one who was slaughtered, there are two views, like their disagreement about the forbearing boy who was given good news of.

The first: that he is Isaac, said by 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Ka'b al-Ahbar, Qatadah and al-Hasan.

Ibn Jurayj said: Abraham slaughtered his son Isaac, who was seven years old, and Sarah had borne him when she was ninety years old.

Regarding the place where he intended to slaughter him, there are three views:

The first: in Mecca, at the Maqam.

The second: at the place of sacrifice in Mina.

The third: in al-Sham, said by Ibn Jurayj, and it is two miles from Bayt al-Maqdis.

When Sarah learned what he intended with Isaac, she remained for two days and died on the day.

The second view: that he is Ishmael, said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, and that he slaughtered him at Mina, near the jimar (stone pillars) at which Iblis was stoned, with seven pebbles at each jamrah, when he opposed him in the slaughter, until he "jamara" before him, meaning hastened, and so they were named jimar.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr related that he slaughtered him upon the rock at the base of Thabir in Mina.

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, this is surely the manifest trial﴾. On this there are two aspects:

The first: the great test, said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: the clear blessing, said by al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Qutrub, and he recited the verse of al-Hutay'ah:

"And indeed their trial, as you know, is in the days, if the trial benefits."

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾. On this there are three views:

The first: that he was ransomed with a ram sent down to him from Thabir, said by Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from him that it was a ram that had grazed in Paradise for forty autumns.

The second: that he was ransomed with a ram from the sheep of this world, said by al-Hasan.

The third: that he was ransomed with a ram sent down to him from Paradise, which was the ram that Habil, son of Adam, offered, and it was accepted from him.

Ibn 'Abbas said: someone who saw the two horns of the ram that Abraham, peace be upon him, slaughtered told me that they were hanging in the Ka'bah.

The word dhibh (with a kasra) means the thing slaughtered, and dhabh (with a fatha) means the act of slaughtering.

Regarding His words, ﴿great﴾, there are five interpretations:

The first: because it had grazed in Paradise, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: because it was slaughtered rightfully, said by al-Hasan.

The third: because of its great bodily size.

The fourth: because of its great blessing.

The fifth: because it was accepted, said by Mujahid.

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And We left for him among later generations﴾. On this there are two views:

The first: the good praise, said by Qatadah.

The first: "I am going to where my Lord has decreed for me."

The second: "I am dying," as one says of someone who has died, "he has gone to Allah, exalted is He." For he, peace be upon him, imagined that he would die by being cast into the fire, according to what was customary for it in destroying whatever was thrown into it, until it was said to it: ﴿O fire, be cool and safe﴾. Then Abraham was saved from it.

Regarding His words, ﴿He will guide me﴾, on this view there are two interpretations:

The first: He will guide me to deliverance from the fire.

The second: to Paradise.

What Abraham said could carry two meanings:

The first: that by his words addressed to the one who threw him into the fire, this would be a warning to them.

The second: that by his words addressed to those among the people who were present and witnessed him, this would be from him a warning to them. This is the interpretation of that according to the view of those who mention that he said it before being thrown into the fire.

The second view: that he said it after his emergence from the fire.

﴿I am going to my Lord﴾. On this view there are three interpretations:

The first: "I am devoted to Allah through my worship," related by al-Naqqash.

The second: "I am going to Him with my heart, my religion and my deeds," said by Qatadah.

The third: "I am emigrating to Him with my self," so he emigrated from the land of Iraq.

Muqatil said: he was the first of creation to emigrate, together with Lot and Sarah.

As for the land to which he emigrated, there are two views: the first, to the land of al-Sham (Syria).

The second, to the land of Harran, related by al-Nasa'i.

Regarding His words, ﴿He will guide me﴾, on this view there are two interpretations:

The first: He will guide me to the words: "Allah is sufficient for me; in Him I put my trust," said by Sulayman.

The second: to the path of emigration, said by Yahya.

This statement of his could carry two meanings:

The first: that by his words addressed to the one who separated from him among his people, this would be a rebuke to them.

The second: that by his words addressed to the one who emigrated with him from his family, this would be from him an encouragement.

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿So We gave him good news of a forbearing boy﴾, meaning: dignified and grave.

Al-Hasan said: "I have never heard that Allah makes lawful for His servants anything more glorious than forbearance."

On this there are two views:

The first: that he is Isaac. Allah, exalted is He, praised no one for forbearance except Isaac and Abraham, said by Qatadah.

The second: that he is Ishmael, and the good news of Isaac's prophethood came after that, said by Amir al-Sha'bi.

Al-Kalbi said: Ishmael was thirteen years older than Isaac.

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And when he reached the age of striving with him﴾. On this there are four aspects:

The first: that he walked with his father, said by Qatadah.

The second: that he reached the age of work with him, said by Ikrimah.

The third: that it is the striving of work by which proof is established, said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: that it is the striving in worship, said by Ibn Zayd.

Ibn 'Abbas said: he fasted and prayed. Have you not heard Allah saying: ﴿and strives for it its striving﴾ [al-Isra' 19]. Al-Farra' and al-Kalbi said: he was thirteen years old on that day.

﴿He said, "O my son, I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you"﴾. Simak related from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The dreams of the prophets are revelation."

﴿So see what you think﴾. He did not say this to him in the manner of consultation regarding the command of Allah, glorified is He. On this there are three aspects:

The first: that he said it to inform him of what Allah, exalted is He, had commanded him, so that he would be more obedient to Him.

The second: that he said it as a test of his patience in the command of Allah, exalted is He.

The third: meaning, "what do you show me of your patience or your distress?" said by al-Farra'.

﴿He said, "O my father, do what you are commanded"﴾, the verse.

On this there are two aspects:

The first: concerning the slaughter, said by Muqatil.

The second: concerning the decree, related by al-Kalbi. So he found him in the test sincere in obedience, swift in response, strong in religion.

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿So when they had both submitted﴾. On this there are two aspects:

The first: that they agreed upon one matter, said by Abu Salih.

The second: that they both surrendered the matter to Allah, exalted is He, which is the view of al-Suddi.

Qatadah said: Ishmael surrendered himself to Allah, and Abraham surrendered his son to Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And he put him down upon his forehead﴾. On this there are three aspects:

The first: its meaning is that he threw him down upon his brow (jabin), said by Ibn 'Abbas. The jabin is the area on either side of the forehead (jabha). The poet said:

"And Abu Hakam put him down upon the brow, so he went to his mother, the abyss."

The second: that he laid him down on his face, said by Mujahid.

The third: that he placed his forehead upon a hillock, said by Qutrub.

Mujahid related from Isaac that he said: "O my father, slaughter me while I am prostrate, and do not look at my face, for perhaps you will have mercy on me and not slaughter me."

﴿And We called to him, "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision"﴾: that is, you did what you saw in the dream. Regarding what he saw, there are three views:

The first: that what he saw was that he took the position of the slaughterer, waiting for the command to carry out the slaughter.

The second: that what he saw was that he was commanded to slaughter him on condition of being empowered, but he was not empowered over him, for it is reported that whenever he struck with the blade, it turned back, and he placed a sheet of copper upon his throat.

The third: that what he saw was that he slaughtered him, and he had indeed done so, but Allah, exalted is He, joined the veins without a separation.

﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾ by pardoning the slaughter of his son.

Regarding the one who was slaughtered, there are two views, like their disagreement about the forbearing boy who was given good news of.

The first: that he is Isaac, said by 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Ka'b al-Ahbar, Qatadah and al-Hasan.

Ibn Jurayj said: Abraham slaughtered his son Isaac, who was seven years old, and Sarah had borne him when she was ninety years old.

Regarding the place where he intended to slaughter him, there are three views:

The first: in Mecca, at the Maqam.

The second: at the place of sacrifice in Mina.

The third: in al-Sham, said by Ibn Jurayj, and it is two miles from Bayt al-Maqdis.

When Sarah learned what he intended with Isaac, she remained for two days and died on the day.

The second view: that he is Ishmael, said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, and that he slaughtered him at Mina, near the jimar (stone pillars) at which Iblis was stoned, with seven pebbles at each jamrah, when he opposed him in the slaughter, until he "jamara" before him, meaning hastened, and so they were named jimar.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr related that he slaughtered him upon the rock at the base of Thabir in Mina.

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, this is surely the manifest trial﴾. On this there are two aspects:

The first: the great test, said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: the clear blessing, said by al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Qutrub, and he recited the verse of al-Hutay'ah:

"And indeed their trial, as you know, is in the days, if the trial benefits."

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾. On this there are three views:

The first: that he was ransomed with a ram sent down to him from Thabir, said by Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from him that it was a ram that had grazed in Paradise for forty autumns.

The second: that he was ransomed with a ram from the sheep of this world, said by al-Hasan.

The third: that he was ransomed with a ram sent down to him from Paradise, which was the ram that Habil, son of Adam, offered, and it was accepted from him.

Ibn 'Abbas said: someone who saw the two horns of the ram that Abraham, peace be upon him, slaughtered told me that they were hanging in the Ka'bah.

The word dhibh (with a kasra) means the thing slaughtered, and dhabh (with a fatha) means the act of slaughtering.

Regarding His words, ﴿great﴾, there are five interpretations:

The first: because it had grazed in Paradise, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: because it was slaughtered rightfully, said by al-Hasan.

The third: because of its great bodily size.

The fourth: because of its great blessing.

The fifth: because it was accepted, said by Mujahid.

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And We left for him among later generations﴾. On this there are two views:

The first: the good praise, said by Qatadah.

The second: it is the greeting of peace upon Abraham, said by 'Ikrimah.

The second: "I am dying," as one says of someone who has died, "he has gone to Allah, exalted is He." For he, peace be upon him, imagined that he would die by being cast into the fire, according to what was customary for it in destroying whatever was thrown into it, until it was said to it: ﴿O fire, be cool and safe﴾. Then Abraham was saved from it.

Regarding His words, ﴿He will guide me﴾, on this view there are two interpretations:

The first: He will guide me to deliverance from the fire.

The second: to Paradise.

What Abraham said could carry two meanings:

The first: that by his words addressed to the one who threw him into the fire, this would be a warning to them.

The second: that by his words addressed to those among the people who were present and witnessed him, this would be from him a warning to them. This is the interpretation of that according to the view of those who mention that he said it before being thrown into the fire.

The second view: that he said it after his emergence from the fire.

﴿I am going to my Lord﴾. On this view there are three interpretations:

The first: "I am devoted to Allah through my worship," related by al-Naqqash.

The second: "I am going to Him with my heart, my religion and my deeds," said by Qatadah.

The third: "I am emigrating to Him with my self," so he emigrated from the land of Iraq.

Muqatil said: he was the first of creation to emigrate, together with Lot and Sarah.

As for the land to which he emigrated, there are two views: the first, to the land of al-Sham (Syria).

The second, to the land of Harran, related by al-Nasa'i.

Regarding His words, ﴿He will guide me﴾, on this view there are two interpretations:

The first: He will guide me to the words: "Allah is sufficient for me; in Him I put my trust," said by Sulayman.

The second: to the path of emigration, said by Yahya.

This statement of his could carry two meanings:

The first: that by his words addressed to the one who separated from him among his people, this would be a rebuke to them.

The second: that by his words addressed to the one who emigrated with him from his family, this would be from him an encouragement.

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿So We gave him good news of a forbearing boy﴾, meaning: dignified and grave.

Al-Hasan said: "I have never heard that Allah makes lawful for His servants anything more glorious than forbearance."

On this there are two views:

The first: that he is Isaac. Allah, exalted is He, praised no one for forbearance except Isaac and Abraham, said by Qatadah.

The second: that he is Ishmael, and the good news of Isaac's prophethood came after that, said by Amir al-Sha'bi.

Al-Kalbi said: Ishmael was thirteen years older than Isaac.

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And when he reached the age of striving with him﴾. On this there are four aspects:

The first: that he walked with his father, said by Qatadah.

The second: that he reached the age of work with him, said by Ikrimah.

The third: that it is the striving of work by which proof is established, said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: that it is the striving in worship, said by Ibn Zayd.

Ibn 'Abbas said: he fasted and prayed. Have you not heard Allah saying: ﴿and strives for it its striving﴾ [al-Isra' 19]. Al-Farra' and al-Kalbi said: he was thirteen years old on that day.

﴿He said, "O my son, I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you"﴾. Simak related from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The dreams of the prophets are revelation."

﴿So see what you think﴾. He did not say this to him in the manner of consultation regarding the command of Allah, glorified is He. On this there are three aspects:

The first: that he said it to inform him of what Allah, exalted is He, had commanded him, so that he would be more obedient to Him.

The second: that he said it as a test of his patience in the command of Allah, exalted is He.

The third: meaning, "what do you show me of your patience or your distress?" said by al-Farra'.

﴿He said, "O my father, do what you are commanded"﴾, the verse.

On this there are two aspects:

The first: concerning the slaughter, said by Muqatil.

The second: concerning the decree, related by al-Kalbi. So he found him in the test sincere in obedience, swift in response, strong in religion.

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿So when they had both submitted﴾. On this there are two aspects:

The first: that they agreed upon one matter, said by Abu Salih.

The second: that they both surrendered the matter to Allah, exalted is He, which is the view of al-Suddi.

Qatadah said: Ishmael surrendered himself to Allah, and Abraham surrendered his son to Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And he put him down upon his forehead﴾. On this there are three aspects:

The first: its meaning is that he threw him down upon his brow (jabin), said by Ibn 'Abbas. The jabin is the area on either side of the forehead (jabha). The poet said:

"And Abu Hakam put him down upon the brow, so he went to his mother, the abyss."

The second: that he laid him down on his face, said by Mujahid.

The third: that he placed his forehead upon a hillock, said by Qutrub.

Mujahid related from Isaac that he said: "O my father, slaughter me while I am prostrate, and do not look at my face, for perhaps you will have mercy on me and not slaughter me."

﴿And We called to him, "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision"﴾: that is, you did what you saw in the dream. Regarding what he saw, there are three views:

The first: that what he saw was that he took the position of the slaughterer, waiting for the command to carry out the slaughter.

The second: that what he saw was that he was commanded to slaughter him on condition of being empowered, but he was not empowered over him, for it is reported that whenever he struck with the blade, it turned back, and he placed a sheet of copper upon his throat.

The third: that what he saw was that he slaughtered him, and he had indeed done so, but Allah, exalted is He, joined the veins without a separation.

﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾ by pardoning the slaughter of his son.

Regarding the one who was slaughtered, there are two views, like their disagreement about the forbearing boy who was given good news of.

The first: that he is Isaac, said by 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Ka'b al-Ahbar, Qatadah and al-Hasan.

Ibn Jurayj said: Abraham slaughtered his son Isaac, who was seven years old, and Sarah had borne him when she was ninety years old.

Regarding the place where he intended to slaughter him, there are three views:

The first: in Mecca, at the Maqam.

The second: at the place of sacrifice in Mina.

The third: in al-Sham, said by Ibn Jurayj, and it is two miles from Bayt al-Maqdis.

When Sarah learned what he intended with Isaac, she remained for two days and died on the day.

The second view: that he is Ishmael, said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, and that he slaughtered him at Mina, near the jimar (stone pillars) at which Iblis was stoned, with seven pebbles at each jamrah, when he opposed him in the slaughter, until he "jamara" before him, meaning hastened, and so they were named jimar.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr related that he slaughtered him upon the rock at the base of Thabir in Mina.

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, this is surely the manifest trial﴾. On this there are two aspects:

The first: the great test, said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: the clear blessing, said by al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Qutrub, and he recited the verse of al-Hutay'ah:

"And indeed their trial, as you know, is in the days, if the trial benefits."

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾. On this there are three views:

The first: that he was ransomed with a ram sent down to him from Thabir, said by Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from him that it was a ram that had grazed in Paradise for forty autumns.

The second: that he was ransomed with a ram from the sheep of this world, said by al-Hasan.

The third: that he was ransomed with a ram sent down to him from Paradise, which was the ram that Habil, son of Adam, offered, and it was accepted from him.

Ibn 'Abbas said: someone who saw the two horns of the ram that Abraham, peace be upon him, slaughtered told me that they were hanging in the Ka'bah.

The word dhibh (with a kasra) means the thing slaughtered, and dhabh (with a fatha) means the act of slaughtering.

Regarding His words, ﴿great﴾, there are five interpretations:

The first: because it had grazed in Paradise, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: because it was slaughtered rightfully, said by al-Hasan.

The third: because of its great bodily size.

The fourth: because of its great blessing.

The fifth: because it was accepted, said by Mujahid.

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And We left for him among later generations﴾. On this there are two views:

The first: the good praise, said by Qatadah.

The second: it is the greeting of peace upon Abraham, said by 'Ikrimah.

The Almighty's words: ﴿And indeed Elias was among the messengers﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

The first: he is Idris. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah, and it is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "and Ibn Idris."

The second: he is from the descendants of Harun (Aaron). This is the view of Muhammad ibn Ishaq. Muqatil said: he is Elias ibn Bahshar. Al-Kalbi said: he is the paternal uncle of al-Yasa' (Elisha).

A group permitted that he is Elias ibn Mudar.

It was said: when the wrongdoings among the Children of Israel grew great after Hizqil (Ezekiel), God sent Elias, peace be upon him, to them as a prophet. Al-Yasa' followed him and believed in him. When the Children of Israel transgressed against him, he asked his Lord to take him to Himself, and He did so. He cut off from him the pleasure of food and drink, and he became with the angels, human and angelic, earthly and heavenly. And God knows best.

The Almighty's words: ﴿Do you call upon Ba'l﴾. Concerning this there are three aspects.

The first: it means "lord" (rabb). This is the view of Ikrimah and Mujahid.

Muqatil said: this is the dialect of the Azd Shanu'ah. Ibn 'Abbas heard a man from the people of Yemen driving a she-camel at Mina, and he said: "Who is the ba'l (owner) of this?" meaning, its lord. From this is the verse of Abu Du'ad:

"And I saw your ba'l in battle, girded with a sword and a spear."

The second: it is an idol called Ba'l, which they worshipped, and Ba'labakk was named after it. This is the view of al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd. Muqatil said: Elias broke it and departed.

The third: it is the name of a woman whom they worshipped. This is the view of Ibn Shajarah.

(p. 65) ﴿And you leave the best of creators﴾. Concerning this there are two aspects.

The first: "the one who is called a creator."

The second: "the best of makers (artisans)," because people make things but do not create them.

The Almighty's words: ﴿Peace be upon Ilyasin﴾. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited: "Salamun 'ala Ali Yasin," with a fatha on the hamza, its elongation, and a kasra on the lam. The rest read with a kasra on the hamza and a sukun on the lam. Al-Hasan recited: "Salamun 'ala Yasin," dropping the alif and the lam. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Salamun 'ala Idrasin," because he read "wa inna Idris la-mina al-mursalin."

As for the one who reads "Ilyas," there are two aspects.

The first: it is a collective noun that includes all of the family of Ilyas, in the sense that each one of his family is called Ilyas.

The second: it is Ilyas, but it was altered by an added letter, because the Arabs alter non-Arabic names by adding letters, as they say Mikal, Mikail and Mikain.

The poet said:

"The people of the market said when we came: 'This, by the Lord of the House, is Israʼin.'"

As for the one who reads "Ali Yasin," in his reading there are two aspects.

The first: they are the family of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: they are the family of Ilyas.

On this view, concerning the entry of the added letter in Yasin there are two aspects.

The first: it was added to match the rhyme of the verses, as in one place He says "Tur Sinaʼ" and in another place "Tur Sinin." On this view, peace is upon his family apart from him, and the attribution to him is an honour for him.

The second: it entered for the collective, so he is included among them, and peace is upon him and upon them.

The first: he is Idris. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah, and it is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "and Ibn Idris."

The second: he is from the descendants of Harun (Aaron). This is the view of Muhammad ibn Ishaq. Muqatil said: he is Elias ibn Bahshar. Al-Kalbi said: he is the paternal uncle of al-Yasa' (Elisha).

A group permitted that he is Elias ibn Mudar.

It was said: when the wrongdoings among the Children of Israel grew great after Hizqil (Ezekiel), God sent Elias, peace be upon him, to them as a prophet. Al-Yasa' followed him and believed in him. When the Children of Israel transgressed against him, he asked his Lord to take him to Himself, and He did so. He cut off from him the pleasure of food and drink, and he became with the angels, human and angelic, earthly and heavenly. And God knows best.

The Almighty's words: ﴿Do you call upon Ba'l﴾. Concerning this there are three aspects.

The first: it means "lord" (rabb). This is the view of Ikrimah and Mujahid.

Muqatil said: this is the dialect of the Azd Shanu'ah. Ibn 'Abbas heard a man from the people of Yemen driving a she-camel at Mina, and he said: "Who is the ba'l (owner) of this?" meaning, its lord. From this is the verse of Abu Du'ad:

"And I saw your ba'l in battle, girded with a sword and a spear."

The second: it is an idol called Ba'l, which they worshipped, and Ba'labakk was named after it. This is the view of al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd. Muqatil said: Elias broke it and departed.

The third: it is the name of a woman whom they worshipped. This is the view of Ibn Shajarah.

(p. 65) ﴿And you leave the best of creators﴾. Concerning this there are two aspects.

The first: "the one who is called a creator."

The second: "the best of makers (artisans)," because people make things but do not create them.

The Almighty's words: ﴿Peace be upon Ilyasin﴾. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited: "Salamun 'ala Ali Yasin," with a fatha on the hamza, its elongation, and a kasra on the lam. The rest read with a kasra on the hamza and a sukun on the lam. Al-Hasan recited: "Salamun 'ala Yasin," dropping the alif and the lam. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Salamun 'ala Idrasin," because he read "wa inna Idris la-mina al-mursalin."

As for the one who reads "Ilyas," there are two aspects.

The first: it is a collective noun that includes all of the family of Ilyas, in the sense that each one of his family is called Ilyas.

The second: it is Ilyas, but it was altered by an added letter, because the Arabs alter non-Arabic names by adding letters, as they say Mikal, Mikail and Mikain.

The poet said:

As for the one who reads "Ali Yasin," in his reading there are two aspects.

The first: they are the family of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: they are the family of Ilyas.

On this view, concerning the entry of the added letter in Yasin there are two aspects.

The first: it was added to match the rhyme of the verses, as in one place He says "Tur Sinaʼ" and in another place "Tur Sinin." On this view, peace is upon his family apart from him, and the attribution to him is an honour for him.

The second: it entered for the collective, so he is included among them, and peace is upon him and upon them.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 37, verse 139–148:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, Yunus was among the messengers﴾. Al-Suddi said: Yunus ibn Matta (Jonah, son of Matta) was a prophet among the prophets of Allah, the Exalted. He sent him to a town called Nineveh, on the bank of the Tigris. Qatadah said: it is from the land of Mosul.

﴿When he fled to the laden ship﴾. The abiq (runaway) is one who flees to a place where he is not known. Al-Hasan said: he fled from his people. He had been warned that if they did not believe, the punishment would come upon them, and he set as its sign his leaving from among them. When he left them, a black wind came to them and they feared it. So they called upon Allah with their children and their animals, and He answered them and turned away the punishment from them. He went out, scheming against his people, angry at the religion of his Lord, until he reached the sea and boarded a ship, which was loaded with cargo. When it began to lurch with them, they feared drowning.

Regarding what they feared drowning by, there are two sayings:

The first: waves of wind that battered them. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: from the fish that confronted them, related by Ibn Isa. At that point they said: "Among us is a wrongdoer; we will not be saved except by casting him off." So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Yunus, and they threw him overboard. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and he drew lots﴾, i.e., he cast lots with arrows. This was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi.

﴿So he was among the losers﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations:

The first: among those who were cast by lot. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

The second: among the defeated. This was said by Said ibn Jubayr, and from it is the verse of Abu Qays:

"We slew the defeated in every direction, and the eyes were cooled by their slaying."

The third: that it means one whose argument is void. This was said by al-Suddi, taken from the expression "dahd al-hujjah" (the refuting of an argument), which means its invalidity. When they cast him into the sea, they believed.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then the fish swallowed him, while he was blameworthy﴾. Ibn Abbas said: Allah, the Exalted, revealed to a fish called al-Lakhm, from the Green Sea, that she should split the seas until she takes Yunus, and that Yunus is not provision for you, but I have made your belly a prison for him. So do not scratch his skin, nor break his bone. Then the fish swallowed him at the moment he was thrown.

Regarding His saying: ﴿while he was blameworthy﴾ there are three interpretations:

The first: that is, he was an offender, a sinner. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: he blamed himself for what he had done. This is the meaning of Qatadah's saying.

The third: he was blamed for what he had done. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The difference between malum (one blamed) and mulim (one who is blameworthy) is that the mulim is one who has done something for which he deserves blame, while the malum is one who has been blamed.

﴿Had it not been that he was of those who glorify (Allah)﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations:

The first: of those who say: "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I was of the wrongdoers." This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: of those who pray. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: of the worshippers. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The fourth: of those who repent. This was said by Qutrub.

It was also said that he repented in ease, so Allah saved him from affliction.

﴿He would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected﴾. Qatadah said: until the Day of Resurrection, until the fish would become a grave for him. Regarding the duration of his stay in the belly of the fish there are four sayings:

The first: part of a day. Al-Sha'bi said: it swallowed him at forenoon and expelled him in the evening.

The second: three days. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: seven days. This was said by Ja'far.

The fourth: forty days. This was said by Abu Malik. It was also said that it carried Yunus until it passed with him to Eilat, then returned in the Tigris to Nineveh.

﴿So We cast him onto the open plain﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations:

The first: onto the shore. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: onto the land. This was said by al-Suddi. Al-Dahhak said: it is a land called Balad.

The third: a place in the land of Yemen.

The fourth: the open space that is not covered by any plant or tree. The poet said:

"I raised a foot whose stumbling I do not fear, and I cast my garments into the open country of the town."

﴿while he was ailing﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

The first: like the state of a child. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: like the state of a chick that has no feathers. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, because he had become weak after strength, and his skin had become thin after firmness.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We caused to grow over him a tree of gourd﴾. Regarding it there are five sayings:

The first: that it is the pumpkin (qar'). This was said by Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: that it is any tree that has no trunk, which remains from winter to summer. This was said by Said ibn Jubayr.

The third: that it is any tree that has broad leaves. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: that it is anything that spreads over the surface of the earth, such as watermelon and cucumber. This was related by al-Qasim ibn Abi Ayyub.

The fifth: that it is a tree which Allah, the Exalted, named yaqtin, which shaded him. This was related by Hilal ibn Hayyan.

It is on the form taf'il from qatana bi-l-makan, meaning he stayed in a place, a temporary stay rather than a firm settlement like the palm and the olive. So Yunus remained under it, eating from it and sheltering by it, until his strength returned to him. Then the tree dried up, and he wept in grief over it. Allah, the Exalted, revealed to him: "Do you weep over the destruction of a tree, and do not weep over the destruction of a hundred thousand or more?" This was related by Ibn Mas'ud.

Said ibn Jubayr also related that when the leaves of the tree fell from him, the sun reached him, and he complained of it. Allah, the Exalted, revealed to him: "O Yunus, you became distressed by the heat of the sun, yet you did not grieve for a hundred thousand or more who repented to Me, so I turned to them."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾. Regarding them there are two sayings:

The first: that he was sent to them after the fish had cast him out. This was said by Ibn Abbas, so he was sent to one people after another.

The second: that he was sent to the earlier ones, and they believed in his law. This is the meaning of Ibn Mas'ud's saying.

Regarding His saying: ﴿or more﴾ there are three interpretations:

The first: that it is for vagueness, as if He said: "We sent him to one of the two numbers."

The second: that it is according to the doubt of the addressees.

The third: that its meaning is "rather, they are more." This was said by Ibn Abbas and a number of the people of interpretation. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿so he was two bow-lengths away or nearer﴾, meaning "rather, nearer." Jarir said:

"Thaʿlabah of the horsemen, or Rabah, you equated with them Tuhayyah and al-Khishab."

The meaning is "Thaʿlabah, rather Rabah."

(p-70) Those who held this view differed on the amount of their excess over one hundred thousand into five sayings:

The first: they are twenty thousand more, related by Ubayy ibn Kab in a marfu' report.

The second: they are thirty thousand more. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: they are some thirty-odd thousand more. This was said by al-Hakam.

The fourth: some forty-odd thousand. This was related by Sufyan ibn Abd Allah al-Basri.

The fifth: seventy thousand. This was said by Said ibn Jubayr.

(p-70) Those who held this view differed on the amount of their excess over one hundred thousand into five sayings:

The first: they are twenty thousand more, related by Ubayy ibn Kab in a marfu' report.

The second: they are thirty thousand more. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: they are some thirty-odd thousand more. This was said by al-Hakam.

The fourth: some forty-odd thousand. This was related by Sufyan ibn Abd Allah al-Basri.

The fifth: seventy thousand. This was said by Said ibn Jubayr.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 37, verse 149–160:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ Regarding this there are three opinions:

First: a clear excuse. This is said by Qatadah.

Second: a clear proof. This is said by Ibn Qutaybah.

Third: a clear book. This is said by al-Kalbi.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship.﴾ Regarding this there are four opinions:

First: it is the association of Satan in the worship of God, Exalted is He, and this is the "kinship" they invented. This is said by al-Hasan.

Second: it is the saying of the Jews of Isfahan that God, Exalted is He, intermarried with the jinn, and so the angels were among their offspring. This is said by Qatadah.

Third: it is the saying of the zindiqs (heretics): that God, Exalted is He, and Iblis are two brothers, and that light, good, and beneficial living creatures are from the creation of God, while darkness, evil, and harmful living creatures are from the creation of Iblis. This is said by al-Kalbi and Atiyyah al-Awfi. (p-71)

Fourth: it is the saying of the polytheists: that the angels are the daughters of God. Abu Bakr said to them: "Then who are their mothers?" They said: "The daughters of the chiefs of the jinn." This is said by Mujahid.

Regarding the naming of the angels as "jinnah" on this interpretation, there are three opinions:

First: they are a clan among the clans of the angels called "al-Jinnah." This is said by Mujahid.

Second: because they are over the gardens (al-jinan). This is said by Abu Salih.

Third: because they are hidden from the eyes, like the hidden jinn.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And the jinnah have certainly known that they will be brought forth.﴾ Regarding "the jinnah" there are two opinions:

One: they are the angels. This is said by al-Suddi.

Second: they are the jinn. This is said by Mujahid.

Regarding what they knew, there are two opinions:

One: they knew that the one who made this claim would be brought forth. This is said by Ali ibn Isa.

Second: they knew that they themselves would be brought forth. This is the view of those who maintain that the jinnah are the jinn.

Regarding His saying "brought forth" (muhdarun) there are two interpretations:

One: for reckoning. This is said by Mujahid.

Second: they will be brought forth into the Fire. This is said by Qatadah.

The second: what Qatadah related, saying: "Men and women used to pray together until the revelation of ﴿There is none of us but has a known station﴾, whereupon the men came forward and the women drew back."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 37, verses 170–179:

The words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And indeed Our word had preceded for Our servants, the messengers﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

First: it preceded with the proofs (hujaj). This was said by al-Suddi.

Second: that they will be given victory. al-Hasan said: "No messenger who brought a law (shari'ah) was ever killed."

﴿Indeed, they are the ones who will be victorious﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

First: with proofs in this world, and with punishment in the Hereafter. This was said by al-Suddi and al-Kalbi.

Second: with triumph, either through faith or through retribution. This is the meaning of the statement of Qatadah.

The words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So turn away from them for a time﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions:

One: the Day of Badr. This was said by al-Suddi.

Second: the conquest of Makkah. This was related by al-Naqqash.

Third: death. This was said by Qatadah.

Fourth: the Day of Resurrection. This is the statement of Zayd ibn Aslam.

Regarding the abrogation (naskh) of this verse there are two opinions:

One: that it is abrogated. This was said by Qatadah.

Second: that it is not abrogated (it remains in force).

The words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And see, for they will see﴾. Regarding this there are four aspects:

One: "See what they have neglected of the command of Allah, for they will see the punishment of Allah that will descend upon them." This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn Zayd.

Second: "See them at the time of victory over them, for they will see what will befall them." Related by Ibn Isa.

Third: "See their condition with your heart, for they will see that on the Day of Resurrection."

Fourth: "Inform them now, for they will know it with certainty (ʿiyan)." This is the meaning of the statement of Tha'lab.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 37, verses 180–182:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe﴾. Al-Sha'bi narrated, saying: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever would like to be given the fullest measure of reward on the Day of Resurrection, let him say, at the end of his sitting when he wishes to rise: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe﴾, ﴿And peace upon the messengers﴾, ﴿And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Lord of Might﴾ may bear two meanings:

One: the Owner of Might.

The second: the Lord of everything that is mighty by virtue of ownership or that is domineering.

﴿And peace upon the messengers﴾ may bear two meanings:

One: His peace upon them, as an honouring of them.

The second: His decree of their safety after their sending, for no prophet was commanded to fight except that he was protected from being killed.

﴿And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ may bear two meanings:

One: for the sending of the prophets as bringers of glad tidings and warners.

The second: for all that He has bestowed upon all of creation.
